subject: p value calculation for bootstrapped parameters

messages.author: 3f3060000990daa6
messages.subject: p value calculation for bootstrapped parameters
parts:
Hi all,

when using se="boot" and retrieving parameters with parameterEstimates, the type of bootstrapped CIs can be adjusted using boot.ci.type.
The p value that is reported, however, is independent of that last parameter (and it does not seem to be the percentile bootstrapped p).

Consider following parameters (bootstrapped with B=1000):


  label   est      se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
1    b4 0.033   0.023 1.484  0.138    0.000    0.086
2     S 0.453 766.930 0.001  1.000    0.054    1.081
3    l1 0.000   0.002 0.000  1.000    0.000    0.004


- The lower 95% CI of the first row is zero, so the p value should be around .05
- The CI of the second row is clearly above zero, but due to the enormous bootstrapped SE the p value is 1.

I have two questions:
1. How is the SE and p value calculated in the bootstrap case?
2. Is there any argument *not* to use the percentile p value, which would treat the second row as "significant"? What is the difference between these two approaches?

Thanks,
Felix

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: p value calculation for bootstrapped parameters
parts:
On 01/31/2013 04:51 PM, Felix Sch�nbrodt wrote:
> I have two questions:
> 1. How is the SE and p value calculated in the bootstrap case?

The SE of a parameter is the standard deviation of this parameter value
in all bootstrap samples. The p-value is based on the est/SE ratio
(similar to a z-test), but here using the bootstrap based SE value. It
is not a percentile based p-value.

> 2. Is there any argument *not* to use the percentile p value, which
> would treat the second row as "significant"? What is the difference
> between these two approaches?

There is currently no argument/switch to change the way the p-value is
computed. (But if anyone sends me a patch to allow for more options, I
would be glad to consider it.)

If you need more flexibility, or you wish to compute your own p-values,
you should use the bootstrapLavaan() function. For example:

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, se="none")
out <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=100L, FUN="coef", verbose=TRUE)

The object 'out' now contains all (100) values for the parameter values.
From here, you can compute any bootstrap based statistic you need.

Yves.
